commit.subject: RISC-V: Probe Svinval extension form ISA string

ai.summary: The series adds support for the Svinval extension, which replaces the single sfence.vma TLB flush with a finer-grained sequence of sfence.w.inval, sinval.vma and sfence.inval.ir instructions, and it was revised from RFC v1 through v3 before a separate KVM RISC-V variant was posted by Anup Patel [1, 5, 6]. Reviewer Anup Patel asked that the extension be probed in riscv_fill_hwcap() so it is detected at boot, and Mayuresh Chitale's later revisions added that probing [2, 3, 5]. Palmer Dabbelt questioned whether splitting sfence.vma helps performance unless independent work is placed between the flush instructions, and suggested the TLB flush operations would need to be split into phases to benefit, but later noted it may be unclear whether the performance characteristics are understood [9]. Mayuresh Chitale replied that the approach resembles the ARM model and is described in the non-normative text of the privileged spec, that the extension is disabled by default and enabled only where the device tree requests it, and that no change to the software TLB model was expected [10]. Alexandre Ghiti asked for benchmark details, and Mayuresh Chitale said no benchmark was run beyond a few stress-ng and kernel selftest runs [11, 12]. Across versions, RFC v2 was rebased on 5.18-rc3 and added the hwcap probe, and RFC v3 fixed the vma used for the sinval instructions and switched to a unified static key mechanism for svinval [3, 5]. The KVM variant was reviewed by Andrew Jones, queued by Anup Patel for 6.1, and Palmer Dabbelt's review thread raised an open IRQ-related question about unresolved feedback from Marc [4, 6, 7, 8].

commit.subject: riscv: Add support for non-coherent devices using zicbom extension

1631ba1259d6.title: riscv: implement Zicbom-based CMO instructions + the t-head variant

ai.summary: The series adds Zicbom-based cache-management operations to the RISC-V kernel, so that non-coherent DMA can be supported on platforms that have the Zicbom extension, and it adds a T-Head variant of those operations for SoCs such as the Allwinner D1 that implement different cache instructions [1, 2, 5]. Reviewers raised whether the block size should be a runtime value taken from firmware rather than L1_CACHE_BYTES, with Anup Patel and Philipp Tomsich debating whether a fixed block size is required for Linux-capable platforms [2, 3, 4]. Palmer Dabbelt asked that the cache instructions be expressed as real assembler mnemonics, and Heiko Stuebner asked whether the T-Head code could go in before binutils support landed, given how long toolchain releases take [5, 6, 23]. Testing by Samuel Holland showed that without the T-Head option MMC, USB and Ethernet broke on the D1, and Corentin Labbe's crypto self-test failure was traced to DMA_FROM_DEVICE mappings invalidating a neighbouring buffer, which Holland attributed to the buffer not being cache-block aligned [9, 10, 11, 13, 14, 31]. Christoph Hellwig asked for the design to default to coherent and mark non-coherent devices, not the reverse, and for ARCH_DMA_MINALIGN and the block-size check to be handled, which led to the dma-noncoherent devicetree property and the device-tree and dma-mapping changes [29, 30, 36, 38, 39, 42, 43]. The series was revised from v1 in March 2022 through v7 in July 2022, with the changes covering the block-size binding, the Kconfig dependencies, cache-line alignment and the coherent-by-default model, and reviewers' tags were collected along the way [24, 26, 41, 48, 51, 52, 54, 55, 56, 57, 58, 59, 60]. Palmer Dabbelt accepted v7 onto the for-next branch, adding an MMU dependency to Zicbom and noting that sparse also needed updating for the new extension [61, 63].

commit.subject: riscv: add ISA extension parsing for Zcmop

164d644059cf.title: Add support for a few Zc* extensions as well as Zcmop

ai.summary: The series adds ISA string parsing, hwprobe export and KVM support for Zimop, Zcmop, Zca, Zcf, Zcd and Zcb, while leaving out Zce, Zcmt and Zcmp [1, 15]. Reviewers asked that the Zc* dependencies on C, F and D be handled in the kernel rather than by requiring devicetrees to list implied extensions, with Conor Dooley objecting to forcing devicetree updates whenever subsets are added [2, 4, 5, 8, 22, 24, 25]. The settled approach was to parse the ISA string in one pass and then validate it in a second pass, with per-extension validate() callbacks that can defer probing, avoiding a general loop to closure [3, 26, 27, 32, 35, 37, 39, 41, 42, 52, 58]. Dooley agreed that the dts churn in patch 2 and the devicetree implication rules would be dropped, and Zimop was merged into the series to remove a dependency [22, 25, 54]. Across versions the series moved from a v1 that depended on Zimop and had no dependency handling, through v2 with dt-bindings validation, to v3 and v4 with the two-phase resolver and deferrable callbacks, v5 which folded in Zimop and reworked the resolution loop, and v6 and v7 which were rebased and changed only extension checks and a rebase onto riscv/for-next [1, 15, 34, 38, 54, 74, 75].

commit.subject: riscv: Implement cmpxchg8/16() using Zabha

ai.summary: Across six versions (v1 2024-05-28 through v6 2024-11-03), Alexandre Ghiti's series added Zacas- and Zabha-based cmpxchg/xchg implementations plus qspinlock support for RISC-V, with Guo Ren contributing the ticket-lock separation and combo-spinlock approach [1, 16, 18]. Reviewers repeatedly raised toolchain compatibility: Conor Dooley argued against enabling experimental extensions by default and Nathan Chancellor flagged clang and GCC build failures and warnings, which led to moving the extension checks into Kconfig and bumping the minimum clang version [2, 3, 6, 17, 52, 68, 69]. Andrea Parri and others reviewed the memory-ordering mappings for fully-ordered cmpxchg/xchg and the ARCH_WEAK_RELEASE_ACQUIRE requirement for qspinlocks, which were revised in later versions [4, 5, 8, 26, 27, 28, 40, 42, 105]. The early-boot ordering problem, where the extension set is not known before spinlocks are used, was discussed at length; Alexandre proposed early ACPI/DT extension parsing as a longer-term fix, and the interim approach used a static key with combo spinlocks [19, 29, 36, 59, 116]. Reviewers asked for ticket-lock/qspinlock selection guidance, code-size measurements, and the Ziccrse dependency, which were added in v4 and v5 [108, 117, 128, 142]. Version 6 was rebased and received final review tags, but after merge a boot failure on QEMU and PolarFire SoC was traced to the static-key switch between qspinlock and ticket-lock interacting with rt_mutex in early boot, and Guo Ren proposed fixes [152, 153, 158, 165, 166].

commit.subject: riscv: add ISA extension parsing for Zacas

188a2122c827.title: riscv: hwprobe: add Zicond, Zam, Zacas and Ztso support

ai.summary: The series, by Clément Léger, adds userspace hwprobe support for the Zicond, Zacas and Ztso RISC-V extensions, which the cover letter says are present in RVA22U64/RVA23U64 and useful to userspace [1]. Conor Dooley questioned whether Zam was ratified, noting the spec listed it as draft and asking if it was truly ratified [2, 4]. Clément acknowledged the assumption had been wrong because the chapter's presence did not mean ratification, and said Zam would be removed [5]. Dooley also NAKed the Zam ISA parsing patch on the basis that the extension was not frozen or ratified [4]. In v2 the Zam patches were dropped, leaving Zicond, Zacas and Ztso, and the cover letter records that Zam was removed because it was not yet ratified [6]. Dooley gave Reviewed-by tags to the Zacas parsing and Ztso parsing patches in v2 [7, 8], and Zacas dt-bindings had earlier received an Acked-by [3].

Conor Dooley's main objection in v1 was that Zam was not ratified, noting that the spec version cited was a draft and asking whether the extension was ratified at all [2, 4]. ai.summary: The series adds runtime detection of the Svnapot extension and uses it for hugetlb pages and huge vmap, with a Kconfig option controlling whether the kernel detects it at all [1, 3, 85, 93]. Reviewers asked for the pte helpers to be restructured, including use of a napot order definition, moving from errata-based patching to a static key and then to alternatives, and fixing checkpatch and build issues such as a missing _PAGE_NAPOT_SHIFT on rv32 and a p4d_clear_huge redefinition [2, 7, 8, 9, 6, 41, 26]. Concerns about the Kconfig default and the memory cost of HUGE_MAX_HSTATE when the option is enabled on hardware without Svnapot were discussed, and were resolved by adding a warning to the Kconfig help text rather than changing the constant [63, 66, 69, 75, 79, 80]. The patches were reworked over time, with the linear-mapping changes split out of the series, the hugetlb code refactored to match arm64-style helpers, reviewer nits folded in, and the series rebased onto the new ISA extension API for v12 and v13 [12, 17, 40, 52, 54, 55, 85, 93, 94].

commit.subject: riscv: add parsing for Zaamo and Zalrsc extensions

35173b666a16.title: riscv: add support for Zaamo and Zalrsc extensions

ai.summary: The series, posted by Clément Léger as v1 on 2024-06-19, adds kernel support for the Zaamo and Zalrsc extensions, which the A extension is now described as being composed of, covering a device-tree binding, ISA string parsing, hwprobe export, and KVM guest support with a selftest update [1]. Conor Dooley acked the devicetree binding and the parsing patches, with his comment on the parsing patch wishing that such fragmentation of extensions did not exist [2, 3]. Charlie Jenkins gave a Reviewed-by for the hwprobe export patch [4]. Anup Patel reviewed the two KVM patches, the guest/VM allowance and the get-reg-list selftest, both on 2024-12-19 [5, 6]. Patel then noted in the cover letter thread that the series conflicted with KVM patches he had queued for Linux 6.14 and asked for an ACK so he could take it through the KVM RISC-V tree, and no version beyond v1 appears in these threads [7].

commit.subject: riscv: Add task switch support for vector

ai.summary: The RISC-V vector (V) extension series, carried by Guo Ren, Greentime Hu and later Andy Chiu across 21 versions, adds Linux kernel support for the V extension: per-task vector register state, sigcontext and ptrace interfaces, and a lazy first-use trap that allocates vector state only when a process first executes a vector instruction [1, 2, 49, 102, 145, 226, 299]. Early reviews centred on the ABI for variable VLEN: a fixed-size sigcontext versus a dynamically sized reserved area, with the consensus moving to a `__riscv_v_ext_state` structure placed after the fp reserved area so as not to break existing layouts [17, 23, 24, 47, 48, 49, 102, 265]. Reviewers also asked for the work to be split into bisectable patches and for toolchain detection and build dependencies to be handled cleanly, which led to the `.option arch` probe and the removal of the unversioned `v` flag from the default `-march` string [16, 90, 124, 134, 145, 296]. A long disagreement between Darius Rad and Greentime Hu about whether vector state should be allocated eagerly per process or requested explicitly, as with AMX on x86, was never fully resolved in the list, and the kernel went with first-use allocation [53, 60, 69, 76, 82, 83, 84]. Concerns about ABI breakage for pre-existing userspace that sees the V HWCAP bit led to the addition of per-process prctl and system-wide sysctl controls, a runtime-adjustable default, and a note that hwprobe reports hardware and kernel support rather than per-process enablement [236, 237, 238, 262, 266, 276, 306, 312, 313]. Versions progressed from v1 (2020) through RFC rounds to v21 in June 2023, which was applied to the Palmer Dabbelt tree; later reports of a signal-frame regression with an unrelated rust build were traced to a sigaltstack bug fixed separately [306, 315, 316, 317].

commit.subject: riscv: add ISA extension parsing for Zilsd and Zclsd

3f0cbfb8a107.title: RISC-V: Add Zilsd/Zclsd support in hwprobe and KVM

ai.summary: The series adds kernel support for the ratified Zilsd (load/store pair) and Zclsd (compressed load/store pair) RISC-V extensions, covering a device tree binding, ISA string parsing, hwprobe exposure, KVM guest handling and selftests, so that user space such as glibc can detect them [1, 7]. In the device tree binding, Conor Dooley asked why Zilsd appeared in the "if" condition at all, and Inochi Amaoto asked whether the Zclsd constraint should use allOf because it requires both Zilsd and Zca [2, 3]. Pincheng Wang proposed simplifying the rv64i condition by dropping the extra "contains" clause, which Conor Dooley agreed to, and accepted that the Zclsd dependency needed allOf [4, 5, 6]. Version 2 incorporated these binding corrections, along with fixing a typo in the patch 1 commit subject, and reviewers Nutty Liu and Conor Dooley then gave Reviewed-by or Acked-by tags to the patches [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13]. Anup Patel's reviews of patches 4 and 5 asked that the new KVM enum values be placed at the end of the enum for UAPI compatibility and that the array entries and config definitions follow alphabetical order; he stated these were handled when he merged them [17, 18]. Paul Walmsley queued the series for v6.19 after cleaning up checkpatch and whitespace issues, and Pincheng Wang later raised merge conflicts from the testing branch with a possible rebase, which was not followed by a v3 in these threads [14, 15, 16].

commit.subject: RISC-V: Add hypervisor extension related CSR defines

ai.summary: The RISC-V KVM series (v1 through v20, Anup Patel) adds initial hypervisor-mode KVM support for RV64 and later RV32 guests, with the VCPU world-switch, ONE_REG register access, in-kernel timer and IPI emulation, and PLIC emulation left to userspace [1, 8, 9, 13, 16, 44]. Reviewers raised substantial points on the series: the interrupt-pending handling and locking, which was reworked to use atomic bitops and a shadow of VSIP, with Paolo Bonzini's suggested fixes adopted [28, 53, 62, 65, 71, 72]; the need for a stable ONE_REG ABI covering the VS CSRs and FP state [16, 17, 36, 39, 59]; and the lack of a timer delta CSR for migration, which was tracked as an open spec issue [48, 49, 135, 136]. Concerns about guest-memory access faulting and the unprivileged-read path were settled by deferring the fix to a later series and adding trap handling with the instruction-length logic [100, 105, 108, 110, 120, 157, 162]. The series also changed substantially across versions: the ISA bitmap and CSR definitions were split out and adjusted [41, 79, 150, 152, 186, 189], the ONE_REG registers were reworked into CORE, CSR and timer groups [112, 153], stage2 page-table programming was simplified to a recursive/iterative form with hugepage and dirty-logging support [169, 200], and the code was moved to and out of drivers/staging while the RISC-V H-extension freeze was pending [218, 222, 251]. In the end the hypervisor specification was reported as frozen, the first two patches went through a shared for-riscv tag that Palmer Dabbelt pulled, and the remaining patches were queued for merging [257, 258, 265, 273].

commit.subject: RISC-V: Enable sstc extension parsing from DT

ai.summary: The Sstc series adds supervisor-level timer compare registers (stimecmp, and vstimecmp for guests) so the kernel can program timer interrupts without an SBI call into M-mode, with KVM also supported [1, 2, 6, 13, 19, 22, 23]. The main objection came from Jessica Clarke, who argued that having KVM write vstimecmp from the SBI set-timer handler changed S-mode-visible state the ratified SBI spec does not allow an SBI call to touch, and that the spec would need fixing first [3, 7]. Atish Patra countered that hypervisor-side hrtimer injection is still possible and offered it as an alternative, while arguing that a stale vstimecmp would cause spurious interrupts if the SBI path did not update it [4, 8]. Anup Patel reviewed the CSR, DT parsing and preference patches and asked for changes to the timer code, including reusing next_cycles and resetting it so an older guest does not get an immediate interrupt, plus a prefix change and a pr_fmt addition [9, 10, 11, 12, 14]. Anup also asked that the new ISA extension enum be moved to the end of the array to preserve UAPI compatibility, which Patra accepted [20, 21]. Patra's final version left the SBI-path vstimecmp update in place as the chosen approach, and the series went from RFC v1 through v2, v3 and v4 with rebases and reworked KVM timer handling, then v5 and v6 with the henvcfg move and enum reordering, and v7 with a compile fix [1, 2, 6, 13, 19, 22, 23]. Palmer Dabbelt merged the non-KVM patches, and after Anup confirmed the KVM dependencies were already upstream and acked the KVM patch, Dabbelt applied it as well [24, 28, 29, 30].

commit.subject: riscv: add RISC-V Svrsw60t59b extension support

59f6acb4be02.title: riscv: Add RISC-V Svrsw60t59b extension support

ai.summary: The series adds Svrsw60t59b-based soft-dirty and userfaultfd write-protect tracking for RISC-V, and early versions gated the PTE bits only on compile-time config, which reviewers challenged [2, 6, 8]. Reviewers asked for the extension's presence to be checked at run time, and Chunyan Zhang agreed, adding per-arch macros pgtable_supports_soft_dirty() and pgtable_supports_uffd_wp() that default to the relevant config options [6, 16, 17, 20, 23, 24]. Other concerns included VM_SOFTDIRTY being set on unsupported hardware, which Palmer Dabbelt raised and which was handled by no longer setting that flag when support is absent [12, 25, 28], the ISA spec link being unavailable at first [11, 13], CI build failures on 32-bit and no-MMU configs [34], a missing dt-binding entry [33, 36, 40], and VMA test breakage that Lorenzo Stoakes reported against v15 [46, 47]. Across versions the series moved from a fixed RFC design (v7) to a dynamically checked design with renamed helpers (v9 through v12), then gained a dt-binding patch and style fixes (v13 and v14), and finally was rebased onto mm-new and given an Acked-by for the dt-binding in v15 [44].

commit.subject: riscv: Detect the Ssqosid extension

5a17eb5f1c4c.title: riscv: add Ssqosid and CBQRI resctrl support

earlier.title: RISC-V: Detect Ssqosid extension and handle sqoscfg CSR

ai.summary: The series adds Ssqosid support (the srmcfg CSR and its context-switch handling) and an initial CBQRI resctrl integration limited to L2/L3 cache capacity allocation, with a DT-based platform driver, and it went through RFC v4 to v6 and v1 to v6 revisions [1, 66, 72, 90, 104, 116, 121]. Sashiko's automated review of each version raised many points, and several were answered by the author rather than changed: the RV32 concerns were settled by requiring 64BIT, since RV32 CBQRI systems were not expected [88]. The suspend/resume state-restore concern was declined because register state is only lost when the power domain is gated, with resctrl reprogramming defaults on resume [72]. The srmcfg fence ordering that was originally added was dropped because Ssqosid does not require it, accepting a brief QoS-tagging inaccuracy at the switch boundary [86]. Reviewers raised the MMIO access width, leading to 32-bit register accesses since the spec only guarantees atomicity for 4-byte accesses [84, 89], and the DT binding was reshaped at Conor Dooley's request, dropping the bare generic compatible and renaming the node and compatible [75, 76, 96]. Reinette Chatre's review of the platform driver asked for RCU-list conventions and for CPU-to-domain association to be derived from each CPU's cache id at hotplug instead of a probe-time mask, which the author adopted for v5 [110, 111, 114, 115]. Monitoring and bandwidth control were deliberately excluded from this series and deferred to a rebase onto the generic schema proposal [1, 66]. Between versions the series changed as follows: v5 moved domain membership to hotplug-time cache-id lookup with RCU list handling, v4 added the PM notifier registration fix and per-controller RCID bounds, v3 renamed the binding and switched to 32-bit accesses, and v6 moved the CBQRI Kconfig block and documented the 32-block limit [104, 116, 121].

commit.subject: RISC-V: Detect Zicond from ISA string

662a601aa355.title: RISC-V: Detect Zicond from ISA string

ai.summary: The Zicond series, which landed as "RISC-V: Detect Zicond from ISA string" across v1 (2023-09-19), v2 (2023-09-25) and v3 (2023-10-03) by Anup Patel, extended KVM RISC-V so guests could discover and use conditional operations, alongside the XVentanaCondOps extension that was eventually dropped [1, 15, 33]. Reviewers asked that the device-tree binding changes be split out from the kernel code, and v2 did this [2, 3, 11, 15]. Several reviewers also questioned whether the Zicond patches were correctly ordered and whether test configurations were needed, and Patel addressed these by reordering the extension list and adding separate test configs [5, 10, 14, 15]. Reviewers including Conor Dooley and Andrew Jones gave Reviewed-by tags to the split patches in v2 [16, 17, 18, 19, 20]. Christoph Hellwig's remark that vendor-specific extensions were out of scope, and Conor Dooley's citation of the patch-acceptance policy, led to the XVentanaCondOps patches being dropped from v3 because Ventana hardware was not yet publicly available, a point Palmer Dabbelt also questioned [21, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32]. Palmer Dabbelt acked the Zicond detection patch and asked for a shared tag to avoid merge conflicts, which Patel provided as a shared branch, and v3 was then queued for Linux 6.7 [34, 35, 36, 38].

commit.subject: RISC-V: Init and Halt Code

ai.summary: The RISC-V Linux port series was posted as v1 by Palmer Dabbelt on 2017-06-28, v7 on 2017-08-01 and v8 on 2017-09-12, with reviewers repeatedly asking for patches to be split up and made bisectable, for better commit descriptions, and for drivers to be moved out of arch/riscv into drivers/ subtrees such as drivers/irqchip, drivers/tty and drivers/clocksource [1, 3, 9, 15, 16, 22, 25, 28, 96, 97]. Reviewers also raised the need for a kernel entry-state document under Documentation/ [6], missing Signed-off-by lines [2], and concerns about the GCC option -mstrict-align, which Palmer Dabbelt agreed to drop after explaining it was a debugging leftover [16, 26]. Reviewers questioned the atomics and memory-ordering implementation, with Peter Zijlstra and Will Deacon noting missing acquire/release bits and the absence of a finalised memory-model specification, which Daniel Lustig said was being revised [84, 85, 125, 127]. Palmer Dabbelt addressed these points by splitting patches, moving drivers, rewriting atomics with _relaxed/_acquire/_release variants, switching the mmiowb approach to a per-CPU flag as suggested by Benjamin Herrenschmidt, and reworking the PLIC driver to use a lock and the FastEOI flow [9, 115, 120, 121, 123, 124, 125, 128]. By v7 and v8 the series had been reduced in size, with several reviewers' remaining comments on Kconfig, timers, the PLIC driver and build infrastructure still under discussion [154, 157, 166, 168, 171, 178].

commit.subject: RISC-V: Add Zicboz detection and block size parsing

7ea5a73617e9.title: RISC-V: Apply Zicboz to clear_page and memset

ai.summary: The Zicboz series, first posted by Andrew Jones as a nine-patch set that also applied Zicboz to memset(), set out to use the cbo.zero instruction to zero memory faster when the extension is present, starting with clear_page() [1, 9]. Reviewers asked about build failures with LLVM and an older GCC toolchain, which were traced to dependencies and resolved in later versions [2, 3, 4], and Jones also revised his memset() measurements after finding a bug in a bpftrace script [5, 6]. Because the memset() case was not yet shown to be a win, Jones dropped those patches and resubmitted as a six-patch series limited to clear_page() [7, 8, 9]. Conor Dooley and Rob Herring reviewed the new cboz-block-size device tree binding, which settled on an explicit property rather than reusing cbom-block-size [10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 16, 20]. Jeff Law reported that Zicboz-based memset helped SPEC2017 on their userspace side, and Jones said he would pursue memset() separately once benchmarks were available [17, 18]. Palmer Dabbelt asked for a fallback to memset() when the block size exceeds a quarter page and for simpler loads, which v4 added, alongside a new alternatives mechanism for patching multiple instructions from assembly and for keying patches on vendor and errata IDs [21, 22, 23, 25, 26, 27]. Ben Dooks found issues when backporting, including the vendor-ID approach not patching in, which led Jones to split the errata ID into separate fields and then to use the upper 16 bits of the patch ID instead of vendor_id in v5 [28, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 39, 40, 41]. Ben Dooks and Sudip Mukherjee reported a clear_page export problem, which was fixed by making clear_page a SYM_FUNC and exporting it in v6 [42, 43, 46, 47, 48, 50]. Dabbelt accepted v6 for for-next and Anup Patel acked the KVM patch [51, 52, 53].

commit.subject: riscv: Add support for Zicbop

ai.summary: The Zicbop series, posted by Alexandre Ghiti as a v3 respin of Guo Ren's lost work, adds Zicbop prefetch instruction support to the RISC-V kernel and then enables the Linux prefetch features on top of it [1]. Reviewers asked for a typo fix, a split of the first patch, zeroing of bits [0:4] in the prefetch instructions, moving PREFETCHW_ASM out of an ifdef, dropping the CBO_ prefix from the prefetch instruction names, and adding a prefetch patch [1]. The changelog records that these comments from v2 were applied, and v2 had itself separated the work from the qspinlock series, adopted reviewer coding-convention advice, added a DEFINE_INSN_S type, and introduced CBO_PREFETCH_I/R/W [1]. Compared with v2, v3 therefore reworks the instruction definitions and the patch layout while keeping the same overall goal [1]. Andrea Parri gave the v3 series a Tested-by tag [2].

commit.subject: arch/riscv: add Zihintpause support

ai.summary: The Zihintpause series adds support for the PAUSE hint in the RISC-V kernel's cpu_relax(), and Dao Lu posted it as v1 through v4 between 2022-05-12 and 2022-06-20 [1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10]. Early reviewers asked for a more informative commit message, noted that the PAUSE encoding is a harmless no-op on CPUs without the extension, and questioned whether runtime probing was needed [1, 3, 4, 5]. Palmer Dabbelt settled the probing question by requiring runtime detection so that platforms without Zihintpause keep executing the div, with the alternatives mechanism suggested as the way to do it [6]. Reviewers then asked for a rebase onto the unified static key mechanism and for cleanup of unrelated changes, which Dao Lu agreed to address [7, 8, 9, 10]. After v4 was reviewed and accepted [11, 12, 16], later messages reported that it broke C=1 sparse builds and module loading with newer binutils, and Samuel Holland argued that a static branch in the widely inlined cpu_relax() was unnecessary and broke builds with CONFIG_CC_OPTIMIZE_FOR_SIZE=y, proposing to run both instructions unconditionally instead [17, 19, 20, 21, 22].

8fe6f7e14c7e.title: RISC-V: Detect AIA CSRs from ISA string

ai.summary: The series adds the Linux irqchip drivers for the RISC-V Advanced Interrupt Architecture (AIA), namely the IMSIC and APLIC controllers and the AIA CSR support, and was posted as v1 through v4 between November 2022 and April 2023 [1, 40, 65, 86]. Reviewers raised a range of concerns: the IMSIC locking needed raw spinlocks because of hardirq-context use (confirmed by lockdep splats) [4, 32]; a warning from the APLIC MSI write path during free_irq was traced to a zeroed MSI message and handled in v2 [6, 29, 40]; the IMSIC compatible string and its naming were debated, with a QEMU-specific string adopted in response to DT maintainers' requests [8, 10, 12, 26, 31, 45]; and the APLIC binding's "interrupts-extended" versus "msi-parent" and "riscv,children" versus "riscv,delegate" properties were repeatedly questioned until the authors explained their roles [9, 27, 33, 34, 61, 62, 63]. The v1 IMSIC driver was also criticised by Marc Zyngier for structure, unnecessary exports, and KVM code mixed in, and a v2 review raised the IOMMU MSI-mapping problem when affinity changes [48, 51, 52]. Some points were left open: the level-sensitive interrupt concern for MSI mode was answered by pointing to the spec's guidance, and a v2 reply indicated the IMSIC driver would be revised with the MSI-affinity fix planned for v3 [49, 53, 52]. Across versions, the series dropped the riscv,slow-ipi property, moved to raw spinlocks, renamed the IMSIC compatible strings and file names, and in v3 and v4 split off the KVM AIA CSR virtualization work into a separate eight-to-nine patch series that was merged in v4 after the SMAIA and SSAIA ISA-string detection patch was acked [33, 40, 65, 86, 93, 94, 95].

commit.subject: RISC-V: Add Svade and Svadu Extensions Support

94a7734d0967.title: Add Svade and Svadu Extensions Support

earlier.title: Add Svadu Extension Support

ai.summary: The Svade and Svadu series adds support for the two PTE A/D bit management schemes, Svade (software-managed, faulting) and Svadu (hardware-updated), to both host and guest kernels in the v5 to v8 patch sets from Yong-Xuan Wang [1, 53]. Reviewers, chiefly Conor Dooley, Anup Patel, Alexandre Ghiti and Andrew Jones, pressed on what the device tree should mean for each combination of Svade and Svadu, and on whether an absent-from-DT case should be read as Svade [2, 5, 6, 7, 11, 18, 19, 23]. The dt-binding wording was settled by Patel's four-case proposal, with Conor Dooley asking for the "Obvious" annotations and the m*id discovery text to be removed, leaving the unknown case to be handled by software being prepared for either behaviour [5, 34, 36, 39]. Reviewers also asked that Svadu be enabled through the SBI FWFT extension, that checks go through riscv_isa_extension_available() rather than ad hoc tests, and that the extension validation use the new .validate callback [8, 12, 30, 32, 48]. Over versions the series moved from v5's direct DT checks to v6's platform-reflecting helpers, v7 corrected alignment and the binding text, and v8 switched PATCH1 to the .validate API, fixed a compile error and added the get-reg-list test change [33, 38, 48, 53]. The series was queued for Linux 6.13 through the RISC-V tree [59].

commit.subject: RISC-V: Detect Smstateen extension

ai.summary: The series adds detection of the Smstateen extension for the host kernel and for guest VCPUs, and extends KVM's ONE_REG interface and VCPU context save/restore to cover senvcfg and sstateen0 [1, 9, 11]. Conor Dooley asked that the cover letter and the first patch explain why only KVM needs Smstateen support and not the kernel, and that the motivation be recorded in the series [5, 7]. Anup Patel responded by quoting the spec's rationale about covert channels between user threads or guest OSes, explained that bit 0 of the stateen CSRs gates access to custom registers, and noted that the kernel does not yet need to manage sstateenX for user tasks [6, 8]. Conor also asked for the DT bindings entry to be split into its own patch, which was done in v3 [4], and he flagged that the first patch could conflict with ongoing work in the riscv tree, which he suggested be shared with that tree [10]. Mayuresh Chitale's changes across versions were: adding the extensions.yaml description and wrapping lines in v2 [2], moving the bindings change into a separate patch and splitting out the senvcfg/sstateen0 save/restore into its own function in v3 [3], expanding the first patch's commit description and rebasing onto kvm_riscv_queue with a reviewed-by tag in v4 [9], and rebasing onto the latest Linux master in v5 [11]. Anup Patel queued the series for Linux 6.7 [12].

a6efe33cc594.title: Svvptc extension to remove preventive sfence.vma

ai.summary: The series, by Alexandre Ghiti, removes the preventive sfence.vma after new vmalloc and new user mappings on harts with Svvptc, handling any resulting trap instead [1, 15, 22]. Reviewers asked for the Svvptc dt-binding to be sent to the devicetree list and for the process to be followed before review proceeded [2]. Andrea Parri asked why the xRET property was needed and asked for the perf gains to be added to the cover letter [3]. Alexandre said the Svvptc authors had removed the xRET behaviour from the extension, so user mappings would take some gratuitous page faults, and he later copied that into the cover letter [4, 5, 15]. Yunhui Cui and Alexandre discussed how to save the registers used by the vmalloc fault check, with Yunhui suggesting thread_info or the kernel stack and Alexandre rejecting the kernel stack and percpu variables [6, 8, 9, 10]. Conor Dooley and Alexandre discussed whether a Kconfig option should bypass alternatives, and Conor argued against it [11, 12, 13, 14]. Anup Patel's review of v3 raised the u64 type, rv32 testing, and a 32-bit atomic, which Alexandre fixed in v4 [17, 18, 19, 22]. Yunhui Cui reviewed v4's vmalloc patch, and Conor Dooley acked and reviewed the binding and probing patches in v3 [20, 21, 23]. The v4 changes were rv32 support, amoswap.w in place of amoswap.d, saving only the needed registers, and a build fix for llvm [22]. A later message from Yaxing Guo reports a case where a stale invalid translation can coexist with a later valid global entry during return to user mode, so the vmalloc check is not reached, and asks whether this is intended or needs a fix [24].

b6fcdb191e36.title: Zbb string optimizations and call support in alternatives

earlier.title: HACK: RISC-V: add zbb support to string functions

ai.summary: The Zbb series adds Zbb-optimised str* routines (strcmp, strlen, strncmp) selectable via alternatives, after a fix-up for call addresses that were wrong once code is patched from another section [1, 2, 4, 15, 16, 18]. Reviewers asked why the EFI stub needed the generic-only marking; the answer was that the stub would otherwise get unresolved references to the Zbb variants, which led to the stub-compilation change [2, 4, 5, 13]. Review questions also covered the auipc/jalr fixup arithmetic, unaligned access in alternative sequences, and the Zbb placement in the extension ordering, which the thread left for a separate reorder [12, 14, 17, 23, 30, 31, 34, 36, 37, 38, 40]. Heiko reworked the approach between versions: v2 introduced cleanup of instruction-parsing helpers and fixed the auipc/jalr patch target [45, 58, 59, 80]; v3 added a funct4 fix and moved the generic-only build flag into the stub and purgatory paths [80, 92]; v4 dropped the inline wrappers in favour of an alternative jump into the generic function, which needed a jal fixup [108, 117]; and v5 split the series into two patches, adopted Andrew's assembly suggestions, and was applied [145, 146, 147, 150].

commit.subject: riscv: Add Zawrs support for spinlocks

earlier.title: riscv: Add Zawrs support for spinlocks

ai.summary: The Zawrs series, first posted as v1 on 2024-03-15 and revised through v3 on 2024-04-26, adds wrs.nto-based waiting to riscv smp_cond_load_relaxed, spinlocks and cmpxchg, plus hwprobe export and KVM guest support [1, 3, 20]. The main reviewer concern, raised by Conor Dooley and Charlie Jenkins, was that wrs.nto is only guaranteed to terminate if the implementation-specific bounded time limit applies or if the hypervisor configures a trap, so an implementation that never terminates could stall a hart waiting on a lock, and the DT binding text was questioned as describing Linux behaviour rather than hardware [4, 5, 6, 8, 12, 15]. Andrew Jones argued that the smp_cond_load condition cannot rely on a store or specific interrupt arriving, that the paravirt alternative was undesirable, and that the spec authors should be informed of the concern [9, 13, 17, 19]. The discussion was settled by Jones taking the concern to RVI ARC, which concluded there was no need for concern because interrupt activity is expected and not locally disabled, while the DT binding was acked in v3 with its Linux-specific wording moved into a code comment [19, 22, 20, 21]. Between versions, the series gained a pause definition, a DT bindings patch, a reworked smp_cond_load based on the Arm approach with the riscv smp_cond_load_acquire dropped, and an updated co-developer attribution, while the Zawrs wait-loop patch was later kept with a non-conflicting hwprobe key and accepted by Palmer Dabbelt after Anup Patel acked the KVM patches [2, 3, 7, 10, 11, 20, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32].

ai.summary: The series, by Evan Green, detects the Zba and Zbb extensions (v2 adds Zbs) and exports them per hart to userspace through hwprobe, with a supporting change that tracks ISA extensions per hart in addition to the cross-hart AND mask used for kernel decisions [1, 10]. Reviewers mostly raised small correctness and style points: a copy-paste error where one define used IMA_ZBB instead of EXT_ZBB, a typo in the documentation, and a request for a blank line before an if statement in riscv_fill_hwcap() [4, 3]. Those were fixed in v2, which also added Zbs, and the fixes were acknowledged in the replies to v2 [10, 11, 12, 13]. A reviewer also noted that Zbs had been left out of v1 and that a reviewed-by tag had been dropped when the patch was revised, and Evan acknowledged both and restored the tag [11, 13]. Palmer Dabbelt applied the three patches to his tree on 2023-06-19 after the v2 reviews, with b4 flagging one reviewed-by trailer whose sender address differed from the From line, and Palmer added it anyway [16, 17, 14]. Reviewers also floated a macro to reduce the repetitive per-extension boilerplate and a question about Zbc, which the thread did not act on [12, 15, 18].

commit.subject: riscv: Add ISA extension parsing for Zalasr

c9651fbc6051.title: riscv: Add Zalasr ISA exntesion support

ai.summary: The Zalasr series adds support for the RISC-V Zalasr extension, which provides real load-acquire and store-release instructions, and its scope grew from four patches in the RFC to ten in v4 [1, 5, 7, 16, 26]. Reviewers raised a central concern that replacing fence-based lowerings with .aq/.rl annotations, or mixing the two, could break the Linux requirement that an unlock followed by a lock provides at least FENCE.TSO ordering, with Andrea Parri proposing options (a) to pair .aq with .rl, (b) to keep fence-based pairing, or (c) to mix them with fence.tso upgrades [8, 14, 17]. Xu Lu's v2 response favoured option (a), while Guo Ren preferred option (c) for its smaller footprint and argued that ld.aq is faster than a load followed by a fence, though Guo Ren also agreed that option (c) is stricter than the .RL-to-.AQ pairing [10, 11, 12, 13, 24, 25]. Xu Lu's v3 settled on applying acquire/release semantics to xchg and cmpxchg, which also needed a change from fence r,rw to fence rw,rw for the acquire fence, and Andrea noted that this affected the read_lock fast path even without Zalasr, which Xu Lu acknowledged as intentional but needing its own commit and changelog [15, 18, 19, 20]. Andrea then asked that the same .AQ/.RL approach be applied to other atomic read-modify-write operations, as arm64 does, and v4 extended the change to arch_atomic operations and removed the arch-specific acquire and release fences [22, 26]. In the v4 review, Andrea asked that any !zalasr lowering changes be isolated in separate patches, and suggested considering smp_cond_load_acquire(), which Paul Walmsley confirmed had only the first four patches applied and that patches 5–8 still await revision, with Xu Lu committing to continue the work [31, 32, 33].

ff689fd21cb1.title: riscv: support for svpbmt and D1 memory types

earlier.title: riscv: Add RISC-V svpbmt extension

ai.summary: The Svpbmt series (v5 through v10, by Heiko Stuebner) adds page-based memory-type support for Svpbmt and the T-Head D1 variant, using an extended alternatives framework that patches code at boot or module load based on detected CPU features and vendor [1, 77, 8]. Reviewers asked for the extension to be spelled out in the cover letter and for the mechanism behind the alternatives choice to be justified, since Atish Patra and Jisheng Zhang both raised static keys as an alternative [4, 9, 12]. Atish's ISA-extension detection replaced the earlier devicetree property, so the series no longer needs its own DT parsing [15, 30]. Christoph Hellwig's review of v8 led to keeping alternatives optional behind Kconfig, wrapping long lines, restyling the assembly, adding a PFN helper, and dropping static globals for vendor data [45, 46, 47, 50, 51, 60, 77, 89]. Reviewers also flagged that boot alternatives must run after the hardware-capability probe, and the series moved them behind fill_hwcap, while the early-boot stage needed for the D1 normal memory type was split out and the compressed-instruction and norelax constraints were added [13, 16, 31, 42, 49, 77]. Across versions the series went from a standalone SBI cache-flush null-pointer fix plus alternatives and Svpbmt (v5, v6) to an isa-extension-based design (v7) with the null-pointer patch dropped in v9, and the final v10 added the early-patching Kconfig option and per-stage compiler flags to fix rv32 and KASAN builds [8, 30, 60, 77, 33, 36].
